title: Monolith or Many

post.author: u/night_shelves_merisel
post.title: I stack shelves on nights at a 24-hour supermarket. At 22:40 one loaf had three prices: £0.55 on the label I'd put up, £0.55 at the self-checkout, £1.10 at the staffed till.

blocks.text: I'm Merisel, night shelf-stacker at a 24-hour supermarket. My shift runs 22:00 to 06:00. At 22:05 the shelf-label printer in the back room gives me the night's new labels, and I put them up first.

Every price in our shop is worked out by a computer program, a list of instructions a machine follows. We have 12 of them, one for each thing that shows or charges a price: the tills, the scales, the label printer and the rest. Each runs on its own, so the team calls them services.

None of them knows a price by itself. Each carries its own copy of the pricing library: a shared set of instructions that takes an item and the time and gives back its price. Think of one recipe card, photocopied for 12 kitchens. Each time the card changes, it gets a new number, its version.
Ysanne's team of three looks after the library at head office. When they change it, they publish the new version: that's a release. Moving one service onto a new release is an upgrade.

An upgrade goes in steps. First they test the service with its new copy in their one test lab, 40 minutes. Then they stop the old copy on the shop's machines and start the new one, which they call a deploy, 10 minutes. Then they check its prices, 10 more. An hour a service, one at a time, because there's one lab.

Version 2.1 came out on Thursday 8 January and ended the January sale. No pricing rule changed after that. 2.2 and 2.3 only tidied the code, so every service stayed on 2.1, and for nine months every copy gave the same answers.

Then head office added a rule: bakery half price after 22:00, reduced to clear, so bread sells before it goes stale. It's in version 2.4 and starts tonight, Thursday 8 October. 2.4 was ready at 14:00. Twelve upgrades is twelve hours, so the last would land at 02:00. The team did the label printer and the self-checkouts first, stopped at 21:00 with seven done, and left five for the morning.
At 22:05 the printer gave me the bakery labels: white loaf, £1.10 crossed out, £0.55. I put them up. The self-checkouts close at 22:30 every night for cleaning.

At 22:40 Dyfrig called me to till 3 over the shop speaker. A woman held a self-checkout receipt from 22:20: white loaf, £0.55. She'd come back for a second loaf; Dyfrig's till charged her £1.10. She pointed at my label. Dyfrig refunded the 55p, and she left both receipts with me, for the manager.
Our duty manager rang Ysanne; she sent this list: each line gives a service, the library version it runs, and its price for the loaf at 22:40.

shelf-label printer     2.4  £0.55
self-checkouts          2.4  £0.55
scales                  2.4  £0.55
online orders           2.4  £0.55
shop app                2.4  £0.55
scan-as-you-shop        2.4  £0.55
reduced-sticker gun     2.4  £0.55
staffed tills           2.1  £1.10
price checker           2.1  £1.10
customer service desk   2.1  £1.10
café till               2.1  £1.10
fuel kiosk              2.1  £1.10
Seven of them knew it was after ten. Five were still living in January.

From 22:00 the seven services on 2.4 charge £0.55 (amber) while the five on 2.1 keep charging £1.10, so the shop has two prices for the same loaf (red) for the rest of the night.

blocks.text: Every program did what its copy told it. Ysanne says that's what scares her. Her team meets on Monday. What should they change before the next pricing rule?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Three counts, then a question. How many copies of the pricing library are in your shop tonight? How many different versions among them? And when Ysanne's team changes one rule, how many upgrades does that take, at an hour each? Copies of one thing slowly getting out of step with each other is called drift. Now the question: on Ysanne's list, what do the five on 2.1 have in common, and which one did the woman at till 3 meet?

replies.author: u/night_shelves_merisel
replies.text: 12 copies, two versions. One rule is 12 upgrades, so 12 hours, and they had 7. The five on 2.1 have nothing in common except that the team hadn't reached them by 21:00. Till 3 is one of the staffed tills.

comments.author: u/tiny_deploys_tirion
comments.text: This is a shared-library problem, and the cure is microservices: many small programs, each deployed on its own, so every team can change its piece without waiting for anyone else. Your library is one big lump that all 12 carry around. Break it up. Give each pricing rule its own small service, and a new rule is one tiny deploy, with nothing else touched. That's how real teams scale.

replies.author: u/night_shelves_merisel
replies.text: Ysanne says splitting the library up has been on her list since spring.

comments.author: u/check_nightly_heledd
comments.text: You'll never stop every slip before it happens, so catch them. Have the shop compare what all 12 services charge for every item, every night, finished by 06:00 when the day manager comes in, and print any item with more than one price. That list would have had your loaf on it.

reply.prompt: Ysanne's team meets on Monday 12 October. What should they change before the next pricing rule? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Work out prices in one place that every till, scale and label printer asks.
options.part2: On Monday 12 October Ysanne's team began moving pricing to one place. By the end of October the library was gone from the 12 services: pricing became one module, a clear inside part of one program, and every till, scale, printer and screen asks it for each price. The shop-floor services joined that program as parts of their own; online orders and the shop app, which the web team runs and which have their own evening rush, stayed separate programs and ask the same pricing module over the shop's network. In the sim, replaying 8 October with one pricing place: one deploy, an hour, and from 22:00 all 12 say £0.55, no mismatch. On Thursday 5 November the next rule went out as one deploy, and at 22:40 Merisel's label, the self-checkouts and Dyfrig's till all agreed.
options.senior: When many programs need the same answer, give the answer one home. A price is one fact about the shop, so work it out in one place that everything asks: a pricing module inside one program, or one pricing service. A rule change is then one test, one deploy and one check, and every till agrees from the same minute. The shape here is a modular monolith: one program, deployed as one, with clear inside parts that talk only through promised interfaces. Split a part out as its own service only where it earns the cost: a separate team that must ship on its own schedule, or a separate load that needs its own machines. Online orders may pass that test; twelve copies of one pricing library never did.

options.text: Split pricing further, into one small program for each rule, so each change is tiny.
options.part2: In October Ysanne's team split pricing into small services, one for each rule, and gave the bakery rule its own. Each of the 12 services then had to be changed to ask the rule services. In the sim, replaying 8 October with one service per rule: 13 deploys, the rule's own service and then the 12 callers, an hour each, 13 hours. With 7 callers changed by 22:00, the loaf still has two prices, and the customer at till 3 still sees £1.10 at 22:40. On Thursday 5 November the next rule needed a new service and the 12 callers all over again, and at 22:40 Dyfrig's till still gave the old answer.
options.senior: Splitting a shared library into one service per rule moves the copies; it does not remove them. Every till still has to know which rules exist and in what order to apply them, so each new rule is a new service plus a change to every caller: 13 deploys instead of 12. Small deploys are good, but the cost that bit here was how many programs must change for one fact, and this option raises it. Microservices usually pay off where a team or a load truly needs to move alone; a pricing rule is neither.

options.text: Print a report each night of every item whose price differs from one till to another.
options.part2: From Friday 9 October a report ran every night, finished by 06:00, listing any item whose price differed between services. In the sim, replaying 8 October with the report on: the customer at till 3 sees the mismatch at 22:40 on Thursday; the report finds it at 06:00 on Friday, 7 hours 20 minutes later, with 5 services differing from the label. On Thursday 5 November the next rule went out to 7 of 12 again by the evening, and Friday's report listed it neatly, after the night's customers had paid.
options.senior: A report that compares prices after the fact is a useful alarm, and finding drift beats not finding it. But it sees the mismatch after customers do, and it changes nothing about why it happens: twelve copies still need twelve upgrades for every rule. Use checks like this to catch what slips through a design, not as the design. Letting staff override the price at the till is the same idea, smaller: it fixes one receipt for whoever complains, while the price checker and the other tills still say £1.10.

options.text: Keep 12 programs, but upgrade all of them together in one go for every new release.
options.verdict: Trade-off: one price, twelve moving as one
options.part2: Ysanne's team built a pipeline: an automatic line that tests all 12 services at once on 12 test machines, then releases all 12 together. In the sim, replaying 8 October: 12 deploys in one run of an hour, and from 22:00 one price, £0.55, everywhere. On Thursday 5 November the café till's tests failed on the new release, and the pipeline held all 12 on the old version. In the sim, the same failure on 8 October: 0 of 12 on 2.4, and £1.10 on the label, at the self-checkouts and at the tills. One price, but the rule started nowhere until the café till's code was fixed the next afternoon.
options.senior: Moving all 12 together does stop the drift: every release lands everywhere at once. But now 12 programs must be tested, released and checked as one, so you pay the costs of many programs (12 test machines, 12 deploys, calls between machines) and of one program (nothing ships until everything passes) at the same time. Engineers call that a distributed monolith. It is an honest stop-gap while pricing moves to one place, and it beats drift, but it is a poor place to stay. And with all 12 changing in the same minute, a bad release reaches every till at once: the blast radius from Canary in the Mine, how much one bad change can hit, is the whole shop.

sim.title: Replay the night of 8 October
sim.lede: You're Ysanne on Thursday 8 October 2026 at 21:50. As given data: 12 services each carry their own copy of the pricing library. Version 2.1 (Thursday 8 January) has no bakery rule; version 2.4 adds bakery half price from 22:00. The white loaf costs £1.10, so £0.55 from 22:00 on a 2.4 copy. An upgrade is 40 minutes of tests in the one test lab, a 10-minute deploy and a 10-minute check: an hour a service, one at a time. 2.4 was ready at 14:00, and by 21:00 seven services ran it, in this order: the shelf-label printer, self-checkouts, scales, online orders, shop app, scan-as-you-shop handsets and reduced-sticker gun. The staffed tills, price checker, customer service desk, café till and fuel kiosk still run 2.1. Until 22:05 the shelf carries the old £1.10 label; at 22:05 the label printer prints the bakery label. At 22:20 a customer buys a loaf at a self-checkout; self-checkouts close at 22:30; at 22:40 she buys a second at staffed till 3. A mismatch is a service whose loaf price differs from the shelf label. Four designs: 12 library copies (as built: 12 deploys a rule, 12 hours); one pricing place every service asks (1 deploy, an hour); a pipeline, an automatic line that tests all 12 at once on 12 test machines and releases them together (12 deploys in one run of an hour, and none move if any test fails); and one service per rule (the rule's own service, then the 12 callers, the services that ask it, changed one at a time: 13 deploys, 13 hours). The nightly report runs at 06:00 on Friday. The till override lets staff key in a different price for one customer. Set the design, how many services are upgraded, the café till's failing test, the report and the override, then step the night in 5-minute steps.
sim.tryThis: Try this: step to 22:00 as built: £0.55 at 7 services, £1.10 at 5, and the old label still says £1.10, so 7 differ from it. At 22:05 the label prints £0.55 and 5 differ. Play on: at 22:40 the customer at till 3 is charged £1.10 against her £0.55 receipt. Set 12 of 12 upgraded: one price, £0.55. Switch to one pricing place: 1 deploy, one price from 22:00 whatever the copies were. Try the pipeline: one price after 12 deploys in one run; now make the café till's test fail: all 12 stay on 2.1 and the label never drops. One service per rule: 13 deploys, and at 7 callers still two prices. Turn on the report: it finds the loaf on Friday at 06:00, 7 h 20 min after the customer did. Turn on the till override: one receipt fixed, still two prices in the shop.

explain.oneLine: No program broke. Each of the 12 services carried its own copy of the pricing library, tonight's rule lived only in version 2.4, and at an hour per upgrade the team of three had reached 7 of 12 when the rule started at 22:00, so the five still on 2.1, the staffed tills among them, charged £1.10 for a loaf every new label said was £0.55.

steps.title: Twelve programs, twelve copies of one library.
steps.text: A library is a set of instructions written once and built into many programs, so each can use it without writing it again. The catch is the word copy: each of the 12 services carries its own. A library upgrade, in steps. First, the team changes the library and publishes a release with a new version number. Second, for each service in turn, they test it with the new copy; what can go wrong: a test fails and that service waits. Third, they deploy it: stop the old copy on the shop's machines, start the new one, and confirm it answers; what can go wrong: the new copy won't start and the old one must go back. Fourth, they check its prices. Then the next service, and the next; what can go wrong: the day runs out, as it did at 21:00 with seven done. One rule change is 12 tests, 12 deploys and 12 checks, and until the last one lands the copies disagree. Copies getting out of step is drift. Segment, below, watched its own library copies drift the same way.

steps.title: Why it never showed in nine months, and why it showed tonight.
steps.text: Version 2.1 came out on Thursday 8 January. 2.2 and 2.3 changed no prices, so nobody upgraded, and it didn't matter: every version gave every item the same price. Half-finished upgrades were harmless because there was nothing for the copies to disagree about. Version 2.4 was the first to change a price. It was ready at 14:00 on 8 October; twelve upgrades at an hour each would have ended at 02:00. By 21:00 the team had done seven, the label printer and the self-checkouts first. At 22:00 the rule started in those seven copies and nowhere else. The label printed at 22:05 came from a 2.4 copy, so it said £0.55; the self-checkout receipt at 22:20, also 2.4, said £0.55; the staffed till at 22:40, on 2.1, said £1.10.

steps.title: One program or many: where a boundary earns its cost.
steps.text: A monolith is one program, tested and deployed as one. A modular monolith is one program with clear inside parts, each talking to the others only through promised interfaces, the contracts between parts from Shapes and Contracts. Microservices are many programs, each deployed on its own. A boundary is a line where one program ends and another begins. It earns its cost when a separate team must ship on its own schedule, or a separate load needs its own machines: online orders, with its own evening rush, might. It costs calls across the network, its own tests and deploys, and copies of any shared code. Canary in the Mine showed how much care one rollout, a release spread out in stages, takes; twelve programs need twelve of them for every rule. Pricing in twelve services bought none of the benefits and paid all of the costs: the boundaries only copied code.

steps.title: Why the other fixes fail.
steps.text: One service per rule moves the copies instead of removing them: the rule's own service plus 12 callers changed to ask it, 13 deploys and 13 hours, and at 7 callers the loaf still has two prices. A nightly report finds the loaf on Friday at 06:00, 7 hours 20 minutes after the customer at till 3 did. A till override fixes one receipt for whoever complains; the price checker and the other staffed tills still say £1.10. One pipeline for all 12 gives one price, but it is a distributed monolith: 12 programs that must move together, so one failing test, the café till's, holds all 12 on 2.1 and the rule starts nowhere.

steps.title: The walk to the staffed till.
steps.text: At 22:40 Merisel left the bakery aisle with the label gun in her pocket and walked to till 3, where Dyfrig stood with the two receipts. Every label she had hung that night was right: it came from a copy of 2.4. The answer was not on the shelves or in the self-checkouts. It was in the five programs nobody had upgraded, and the first of them was the staffed till in front of her, still working out prices the way it had since 8 January.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for the next pricing rule. Four boxes along the top: staffed tills, self-checkouts, the label printer and 9 more services, 12 in all. Each asks one pricing module below for every price and gets £0.55 for the loaf from 22:00. The pricing module holds the only copy of the pricing rules, version 2.4, and a rule change is one deploy, one hour.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the next pricing rule. All 12 services ask one pricing module for every price, so the bakery rule lives in one copy, version 2.4. One deploy of an hour reaches every till, scale and label at once, and from 22:00 the loaf is £0.55 everywhere.

fix.title: The fix: one home for every price, and boundaries only where a team or a load needs them
fix.text: Take the pricing library out of the 12 services and make it one pricing module inside one program, with the shop-floor services as clear inside parts of that program. Every till, scale, label printer and screen asks the module for each price. A new rule is then one release, one test, one deploy and one check: an hour, with every service agreeing from the same minute. Keep a part as its own program only where it earns it: online orders and the shop app, run by the web team with their own evening rush, can stay separate, but they ask the same pricing module instead of carrying a copy. Write down which team owns the module and which interface every caller uses, so a change to the rules never needs a change to the callers.

limits: One pricing place is one thing that must not go down: if it stops, every till stops pricing. It needs a standby copy of the module ready to take over, and tills may keep the last answers for a few minutes for an outage, as long as those saved answers expire.

Merging services into one program means one release rhythm: the shop-floor parts ship together, so a slow part can hold up a fast one. The clear inside parts keep that manageable, and a part that truly needs its own schedule can be split out later along a line that already exists.
The right boundaries change as the shop changes. If online orders grows a load or a team of its own, splitting it out may start to earn its cost; review the lines when that happens, not before.

explain.seniorTake: One program or many is not a matter of taste or fashion; it is a question of what has to change together. Facts that must agree everywhere, like a price, belong in one place that everything asks. Lines between programs are worth drawing where something truly differs: a team that must ship on its own schedule, a load that needs its own machines. Every line has a price: calls across the network, separate tests and deploys, and copies of whatever code both sides share. A shared library copied into many services is the quiet version of that price: it costs nothing for months, then one rule change shows you every copy at once. Start with one program and clear inside parts, and split a part out when it earns it; it is easier to cut along a line that is already clean than to glue twelve programs back together.

realWorld.title: Segment, 2018: shared libraries, copied
realWorld.text: Noonan writes that, as Segment's services multiplied, "we created shared libraries to make common transforms and functionality" available to every destination service. A destination is a place Segment sends its customers' data. Then: "Over time, the versions of these shared libraries began to diverge across the different destination codebases." That is drift, the same as the pricing library's 2.1 and 2.4.

realWorld.title: Segment: one change, every service
realWorld.text: The post says "Testing and deploying changes to these shared libraries impacted all of our destinations." and "Eventually, all of them were using different versions of these shared libraries." Each library change meant an upgrade per service, as Ysanne's twelve hours did.

realWorld.title: Segment: a small team, back to one service
realWorld.text: The team was down to "3 full-time engineers spending most of their time just keeping the system alive". Their fix: "The first item on the list was to consolidate the now over 140 services into a single service." The post is honest about the cost, listing among the trade-offs "Fault isolation is difficult.": one bug can now affect every destination at once.

realWorld.title: Shopify, 2019: a modular monolith
realWorld.text: Westeinde writes: "A modular monolith is a system where all of the code powers a single application and there are strictly enforced boundaries between different domains." A domain is one area of the business, like pricing. Shopify chose it because "We wanted a solution that increased modularity without increasing the number of deployment units".

realWorld.title: Shopify: one place to run
realWorld.text: The same post notes a plain benefit of one program: "Since monoliths are deployed to one place, only one set of infrastructure needs to be managed." Infrastructure is the machines and settings a program runs on; twelve services need twelve sets of it.

asked: Monolith or microservices for a new product?
How do you decide where a service boundary goes?
interview.answer: For a new product I'd usually start with one program, a modular monolith: deployed as one, with clear inside parts for each area, such as pricing, orders and accounts, that talk to each other only through promised interfaces. That gives one test run, one deploy and one place for every shared fact, while keeping the parts separate enough to cut out later. I'd draw a service boundary, a line where one program ends and another begins, only where it earns its cost. Two reasons usually do: a separate team that must ship on its own schedule, or a separate load that needs its own machines and its own scaling. Each boundary costs calls across the network, separate tests and deploys, and copies of shared code, so I'd watch for two warning signs. One is a shared library copied into many services, because the copies drift and one rule change becomes many upgrades. The other is services that must always be released together, which is a distributed monolith: the costs of many programs and of one. I'd tell the story of a supermarket whose 12 services each carried a copy of the pricing library: a new half-price rule reached 7 of 12 before it started, so one loaf had two prices while five programs, the staffed tills among them, still ran the old copy. The fix was one pricing module that every till asks.

atWork: Find a library that is copied into several of your services; a pricing, tax, sign-in or formatting library is a common pattern. List every service that carries it and the version each one runs today. More than one version means drift, even if nothing has gone wrong yet. Then ask three questions. When this library changes, how many deploys does that take, and how long until the last one lands? Does the logic belong in one place that every service asks, as one module or one service, instead of in copies? And does each service boundary in that area earn its cost: a separate team, or a separate load? If several services must always be released together, write that down as a distributed monolith and plan how to bring them together or truly separate them. On AWS, Amazon's cloud, the dependency list built into each Lambda function or container image is where the versions show; a small script that lists them side by side often finds the drift. Standards: if your company is pursuing SOC 2 and includes processing integrity (the PI1 criteria), an auditor would look for evidence that processing is complete, valid, accurate and timely: for a shop, that the price charged matches the price shown. Two copies of one pricing rule giving two answers is exactly what that evidence must rule out, so build one source for each price into the first draft of the design, not at audit time. This is not audit advice.

recall.prompt: Your company runs 20 services, and the same sign-in library is built into every one of them. Security asks for a change to how passwords are checked. Three weeks later 14 services run the new version and 6 the old, and one customer is locked out of one app and not another. What went wrong, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Each service carries its own copy of the library, so copies drift: one change needs every service upgraded, and until the last one lands they disagree
Put the shared logic in one place every service asks, one module in one program or one service, so a change is one deploy
Draw service boundaries only where a team or a load truly differs; releasing all 20 together would be a distributed monolith

recall.model: Each of the 20 services carries its own copy of the sign-in library, so the copies drift: one change needs every service upgraded, one deploy at a time, and until the last one lands the services run different versions and disagree about the same customer. I'd move the password check to one place every service asks, one module in one program or one sign-in service, so the next change is one deploy and every app agrees from the same minute. I'd keep separate services only where a separate team or a separate load needs them, and I wouldn't settle for a pipeline that releases all 20 together: that's a distributed monolith, with the costs of many programs and of one.

recall.prompt: In the sim, replaying 8 October with 7 of 12 services upgraded, which design gives every till, scale and label the same loaf price from 22:00 with a single deploy?
options: One pricing place every service asks
recall.why: One pricing place needs 1 deploy of an hour, and from 22:00 all 12 services say £0.55. As built, 7 copies say £0.55 and 5 say £1.10. The pipeline also gives one price, but it takes 12 deploys in one run, and one failing test holds all 12. One service per rule takes 13 deploys, and with 7 callers changed the loaf still has two prices.

recall.prompt: Ysanne's pipeline tests all 12 services and releases them together. The café till's test fails on the new release. What happens, and what is this design called?
options: Only the café till stays on the old version; microservices
All 12 stay on the old version; a distributed monolith
Every service except the café till moves; a monolith
All 12 move and the café till is fixed later; a pipeline
recall.why: The pipeline releases all 12 or none, so one failing test holds every service on 2.1 and the rule starts nowhere. Many programs that must always move together are a distributed monolith: the costs of many programs and of one at the same time.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: for a new product, would you build a monolith or microservices, and how do you decide where a service boundary goes?

keyIdeas.idea: Usually start with one program with clear inside parts, a modular monolith, deployed as one
Draw a boundary where a separate team or a separate load needs to move alone
Shared facts live in one place; copied shared libraries drift, and services that must be released together are a distributed monolith

recall.model: I'd usually start with one program, a modular monolith: deployed as one, with clear inside parts that talk through promised interfaces. I'd split a part out only where it earns the cost: a separate team that must ship on its own schedule, or a separate load that needs its own machines. Shared facts, like a price, should live in one place that everything asks; a shared library copied into many services will drift, and services that must always be released together are a distributed monolith, paying the costs of many programs and of one.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 2 months later. Pricing lives in one place now. Every till, scale and label printer asks the pricing module inside the shop-floor program; online orders and the shop app stayed separate and ask the same module over the network. The 5 November rule went out in one deploy and every price agreed. Then on Friday 27 November, the biggest online sale of the year, online orders ran at ten times a normal evening from 20:00. Every basket on the website asked the pricing module again each time a customer changed it. From 20:10 the staffed tills took 6 seconds to price each scan instead of under one, and queues reached the bakery aisle. Every price was still right.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Prices still agree everywhere. Why did the tills slow on 27 November, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: The tills and the online rush share one pricing module on the same machines, so online orders' separate load slowed the shop floor
A separate load is where a boundary earns its cost: run the online side's pricing on its own machines, from the same code and the same release, so prices still agree
Protect the tills: limit how often online baskets ask, or let a basket keep its prices for a few minutes

coldCase.model: The prices were right because there is one pricing module, but the tills and the online rush now share it on the same machines. Online orders' evening load jumped tenfold, every basket change asked again, and the shop floor queued behind it. That's the case where a boundary earns its cost: a separate load. I'd run the pricing module for the online side on its own machines, built from the same code and shipped in the same release, so there is still one set of rules and every price agrees, while the tills keep their own machines. And I'd protect the tills further: limit how often an online basket may ask, or let a basket keep its prices for a few minutes, so a sale on the website can't slow a loaf at till 3.
